newsitem.title: USA: Commerce challenges U.S., Irish businesses.
newsitem.headline: Commerce challenges U.S., Irish businesses.

text.p: Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor on Monday challenged U.S. and Irish business leaders to form a business development council to promote investment in Northern Ireland and the six border counties, saying economic strength will help bring peace to the region.

"You can't have peace without economic development and you can't have economic development without peace," Kantor said in a brief interview with Reuters. "They're tied at the hip ... you can't have a successful peace process unless you create a good economy."
Kantor made his comments during the Commerce Department's Conference for Trade & Investment in Northern Ireland and the Border Counties of Ireland, held this week in Pittsburgh.

The conference included about 200 companies from the United States, Northern Ireland and the border counties, whose representatives discussed investment possibilities that included joint ventures, trade opportunities and U.S. investment in the region in the form of new facilities.
Saying "a lot of business" should result from the conference, Kantor challenged business leaders from all three regions to form a council to identify business opportunities.

"(Business investment) is a critical aspect (for peace,") Kantor said. "Frankly, you can't attract investment if you have an unstable political situation. But in order to have (stability) you have to be growing jobs, growing incomes, attracting investment and engaging in trade."
Kantor said U.S. investment has grown by $1.6 billion in Northern Ireland and by $230 million in the border counties since the Clinton administration began economic initiatives in the regions.

Ron Brown, the late commerce secretary who died earlier this year in a plane crash in Bosnia, in December 1994 led a delegation of U.S. business representatives to participate in British Prime Minister John Major's investment conference in Belfast.

In May 1995, the White House Conference for Trade and Investment in Ireland took place in Washington. Brown then accompanied President Clinton to Northern Ireland later that year, marking the first time a U.S. president has travelled there.
